items.title: AWS Ships Kiro Bots: Persistent Coding Agents With Their Own Memory and Schedules
items.summary: AWS made Kiro Bots generally available on November 5 inside Kiro Crew, its open-source multi-agent coding workspace. Each bot is a named, long-running agent that owns one slice of a developer's workflow (CI watching, issue triage, release checks), keeps separate persistent memory ('Notes'), spawns parallel worker sessions, and runs on conversational schedules such as 'check CI every 30 minutes' or 'draft release notes every Friday.' Permissions are scoped per bot, and different models can be mixed for planning vs. workers. AWS frames the shift as 'from task delegation to process delegation.'
items.impact: Coding agents are graduating from one-shot sessions to standing, scheduled jobs with memory — the same pattern operators run with cron and CI, now agent-native. The real watch-items are a 'coordination tax' (scheduled bots burn credits 24/7) and auditability (why did a bot decide X across weeks of notes?). Teams should scope bots to one job, keep merge/deploy rights with humans, and meter cost before scaling.

items.title: Cognition Releases SWE-2 Flash: a 276B Coding Model at One-Fifth the Price of SWE-2
items.summary: On November 4, Cognition released SWE-2 Flash, a coding model built on Thinking Machines' Inkling-Small (276B total / 12B active parameters, MoE). A mid-training stage plus RL lifted Terminal-Bench 4.0 pass rate from 0.9% to 20.0% and FrontierCode 2.0 from 3.2% to 24.0% over the base. Cognition reports ~3x the speed of SWE-2 at one-fifth the price; it runs in Devin Desktop and CLI (free through Nov 30, then 1/5 SWE-2 pricing). Weights stay private for now.
items.impact: A clear signal in the 'smaller, cheaper, specialized' coding-model race: a mid-training step on code/science corpora can unlock large benchmark gains without frontier-scale spend. For teams, the takeaway is that cost-per-task — not just raw capability — is becoming the differentiator in production coding agents.

items.title: GitHub Formalizes the Agentic Coding Workflow — and Pushes Copilot Into Xcode and JetBrains Air
items.summary: GitHub's November guidance formalizes agentic coding around four stages — Plan, Build, Verify, Observe — and reports 1.2B weekly commits in October (400%+ YoY) alongside a finding that pull requests sat 441% longer in review as AI adoption rose. In parallel, Copilot landed in Xcode's built-in coding assistant (public preview, Nov 4) and inside JetBrains Air via the Agent Client Protocol (Nov 3), while the @GitHub bot for Slack/Teams reached GA (Nov 6), able to open issues and PRs straight from a chat thread.
items.impact: The bottleneck is moving from generation to coordination and verification. More commits do not equal more productivity when review queues balloon; the winning setup is defined roles, current context, explicit authority, and independent verification — not just a stronger model. ACP looks set to become the standard 'socket' for coding agents inside editors, much like LSP did for language tooling.

items.title: At the China International Import Expo, Embodied Intelligence Moves From 'Performances' to Real Service
items.summary: At the 9th CIIE (Nov 5-6, Shanghai), humanoid robots shifted from demo stunts (dancing, sparring) to practical work — hotel concierge, luggage carrying, tea service, and on-site photo printing. The parallel Hongqiao Forum on humanoid robots released the '2026 Humanoid Robot Application Scenario Atlas' covering ten domains (manufacturing, public services, special operations, agriculture). Industry leaders converged on a thesis: embodied progress comes from co-evolving 'body' and 'brain,' and the hardest gap is the 'last few millimeters' of alignment between AI and the physical world — a problem several predicted could close within 1-2 years via self-improving data flywheels.
items.impact: The narrative for humanoids is maturing from spectacle to deployable value, backed by an authoritative scenario map that helps match supply and demand. For builders, the consensus that hardware embodiment caps generalization — and that real-world data loops are the core driver — reframes where to invest (sim-to-real, edge inference, dexterous end-effectors).

items.title: Industry Report: Over 60% of Humanoids Still Stuck in Demos, Only ~8% in Real Factories
items.source: Xinhua Finance / China Financial Information Service
items.summary: The '2026 Embodied Intelligence Industry Innovation Report' (released Nov 5-6) finds the sector moving from development demos toward real-world continuous operation, but with a stark gap: only about 8% of humanoids have entered manufacturing or warehousing, while over 60% remain in exhibitions, commercial shows, or research/teaching. Yet supply is scaling fast — H1 2026 global humanoid shipments exceeded 22,000 units, up nearly 300% YoY, and daily rental prices have fallen below 1,000 yuan. Bright spots exist: Galbot S1 runs 7x24 on CATL's line; 15 Leju 'Kuafu' robots hit 98% success over ~1,000 hours at Zhaofeng; Zhisquare signed a ~500M yuan, 1,000-unit, 3-year order with HKC.
items.impact: The metric that matters is shifting from 'how many shipped' to 'how many run continuously and deliver results.' Reliability engineering — not flashy skills — is the binding constraint (hidden degradation of tendons/sensors only shows under 24/7 load). Buyers now ask about repeatability, payload, deployment time, and stable uptime, signaling a market pivot from novelty to operational units.
